relations.myth: Advice to petition Varuṇa for a son
relations.note: Nārada advises the childless Hariścandra to seek a son from Varuṇa.

relations.myth: Rohita granted for a sacrificial promise
relations.note: Varuṇa grants Hariścandra a son in exchange for promising the child as sacrifice.

relations.myth: Punishment for delaying the promised sacrifice
relations.note: Varuṇa afflicts Hariścandra with abdominal swelling after repeated postponement of Rohita's sacrifice.

relations.myth: Release of Śunaḥśepa and royal cure
relations.note: After the substitute is released, Varuṇa's affliction ends and Hariścandra is cured.
Rohita is Hariścandra's son and successor in Vedic, Purāṇic, and regional traditions.

relations.myth: Rohita promised as Varuṇa's human victim
relations.note: Hariścandra promises his son as sacrifice, repeatedly delays, then accepts Śunaḥśepa as substitute.
Hariścandra sells Rohitāśva with Śaivyā to meet Viśvāmitra's demanded priestly fee.
Hariścandra's intended self-immolation precedes divine restoration of his dead son and installation as king.
Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, repeatedly persuades Rohita to keep wandering while Hariścandra remains afflicted.
Indra appears with the gods when Rohitāśva is restored and Hariścandra is offered heaven.
Epic and Purāṇic traditions place Hariścandra in Indra's heaven or give him Indra's chariot.
Hariścandra accepts Ajīgarta's sold middle son as substitute victim at the royal sacrifice.
Hariścandra accepts the purchased Śunaḥśepa, who is bound for sacrifice before hymns secure his release.
Viśvāmitra serves among the ritual priests in versions of the Śunaḥśepa sacrifice.
Viśvāmitra wagers with Vasiṣṭha that he can expose or defeat Hariścandra's celebrated truthfulness.
Viśvāmitra takes Hariścandra's kingdom, demands further payment, and drives the sale of his family and self.
Vasiṣṭha belongs to the defined priestly team officiating at Hariścandra's sacrifice.
Vasiṣṭha praises his patron Hariścandra and stakes ascetic merit upon the king's truthfulness.
Jamadagni officiates as adhvaryu at Hariścandra's sacrifice without a separate adventure.
Ayāsya serves as Sāman-chanter during Hariścandra's sacrifice.
Vāmadeva participates in the debate following the release of Hariścandra's substitute victim.
Hariścandra serves Dharma unknowingly while Dharma assumes the form of his caṇḍāla master.
Dharma reveals his disguise and vindicates Hariścandra after the king completes the ordeal.

relations.myth: Infernal authority in the cremation-ground dream
relations.note: Yama's messengers and infernal authority appear within Hariścandra's dream of punishment and rebirth.
Regional tellings sometimes replace Dharma with Yama as Hariścandra's disguised caṇḍāla master.
Hariścandra meditates upon the formless Viṣṇu or Brahman at the culmination of his ordeal.
Some modern retellings make Viṣṇu appear personally to end Hariścandra's ordeal.
The Śākta redaction makes the Goddess the power and object of Hariścandra's ultimate salvation.
Some later theatre and film endings make Śiva appear among those ending Hariścandra's ordeal.
The Viśvedevas are drawn into the narrative frame surrounding Hariścandra's intervention and Viśvāmitra's curse.
Triśaṅku is Hariścandra's father in the dominant Purāṇic solar-dynasty genealogy.
Śaivyā is Hariścandra's queen in Sanskrit ordeal narratives, with regional names Tārāmatī and Candramatī.
Hariścandra reluctantly sells his wife into domestic servitude to satisfy Viśvāmitra's demanded fee.

relations.myth: Recognition and attempted death on son's pyre
relations.note: The estranged spouses recognize each other and resolve to die together upon their son's pyre.
Harita is Hariścandra's later descendant through Rohita in the dominant Purāṇic genealogy.
Cañcu or Campaka belongs to the later descendant line traced from Hariścandra.
Govindarāja identifies Hariścandra with the Rāmāyaṇa's purchasing king Ambarīṣa to reconcile conflicting accounts.

relations.myth: Double narrative of Hariścandra and Nala
relations.note: A Telugu śleṣa poem simultaneously narrates both kings, though they never meet within an ancient myth.
